title: The hard questions, looking back
hook: suffering, doubt, grief, and love entering them
tomorrow: what promise does Matthew make on page one, and keep at the end?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Revelation: told of a lion, John sees a slain Lamb, and the city at the end keeps its gates open. The line was all things new.

The worst texts arrive at ordinary times. Can you talk? And then the news: a diagnosis, a death, a family coming apart. What comes to mind first often sounds wrong out loud. Everything happens for a reason. At least it isn't worse. John's Gospel has a strange detail about a moment like that. Before Jesus even reaches Bethany, he tells his friends he is going to wake Lazarus out of sleep. He knows how this ends. So why, at the grave, does he cry?
screen: `CAN YOU TALK?` → `WHAT DO YOU SAY?` → `HE KNOWS HOW IT ENDS. SO WHY CRY?`

segments.voice: Watch the scene. Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. His sister Mary falls at Jesus's feet: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Her sister Martha said the very same words before her. It isn't a polite question. It's grief, said straight to his face. Jesus doesn't correct her or explain. He sees her weeping, and the mourners with her, and he is troubled. Then the verse: "Jesus wept." In the King James, that's all of it. So the puzzle has its answer. The tears aren't about the ending. They're for the people in front of him. Love walks into the grief before anything gets fixed. Looking back, this path has met the hard questions that way. The Bible keeps them in plain sight. A psalm opens, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" and in Matthew and Mark, Jesus cries those words from the cross. A father begging Jesus to heal his son says, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Belief and doubt in one breath, and he isn't sent away. Christians have offered different answers to why suffering exists, and they don't agree on one; some say the honest answer is that we don't know. But the stories share a shape. Love enters.
screen: `IF THOU HADST BEEN HERE.` · `JESUS WEPT.` · `MY GOD, WHY?` · `HELP THOU MINE UNBELIEF.` · then, large: `LOVE ENTERS.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees. Set one hard question you carry there, about a loss, a suffering or a doubt, and don't try to solve it; just breathe beside it, the way Mary brought her grief to Jesus's feet. If the weight ever feels dangerous, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
The hard questions. Suffering, doubt and grief, met not with a neat answer but with love walking in, the way Jesus wept at a friend's tomb.
Keep this: love enters, not to explain the grief, but to be there inside it. Rest well.

howItsDone: Christians bring hard questions to God in prayer, sometimes in the psalms of lament, and churches hold funerals and pastoral visits where people can grieve without being handed quick answers.

fork.setup: your little brother asks: if Jesus knew he'd bring Lazarus back, why did he cry at the grave?
options: because he wasn't sure it would work this time.
because he loved them, and grief was in the room.
because the crowd expected some tears from him.
fork.reveal: John says he saw Mary weeping, and the mourners, and was troubled. the tears were for the people in front of him: love enters the grief before anything is fixed.

original.note: Greek: wept, shed tears. in John 11:35 the verse is this verb and Jesus's name.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means having an answer for every hard question.
what it means: the Bible keeps grief and doubt in plain sight, and meets them with love walking in.
what a scholar hears: John 11:35 uses ἐδάκρυσεν, shed tears; the mourners in 11:33 are weeping aloud, κλαίοντας, a different verb.
guess: grief, doubt and suffering, met by love, not answers
riddles in the Bible scholars have never solved
questions you must settle before you can believe

chat.says: nia finally texted back. her parents are splitting up. that's why. what do i even say?
options: Don't explain it. Go sit with her. Jesus wept with Mary before he fixed anything.
Tell her everything happens for a reason, and God has a plan in all of it.
Give her space. Grief is private, and showing up would only make it harder.
chat.meaning: At Lazarus's tomb Jesus doesn't argue with Mary's grief or explain it. He weeps with her. Love enters before anything is fixed.

Lazarus.meaning: Mary and Martha's brother, called out of his tomb

Bethany.meaning: the village near Jerusalem where Lazarus lived

Martha.meaning: Lazarus's sister, who met Jesus on the road first

mourners.meaning: people who came to weep with the family
